title: When AI Runs the Business: The Reality of Enterprise-Wide Automation

segments.text: The next session is starting. >> [snorts] >> So, please take your seats. Okay. Uh when AI runs uh the business, the reality of enterprise-wide
automation, uh we talked the whole day today about AI enablement in enterprise transformation. So, AI helping also the business itself. Uh this session is about
running AI itself within the enterprise. Leading this session will be uh Enis Erker, uh deputy editor-in-chief at Forbes, Austria. Co-speaker, Axel Shell, CTO of Allianz
Technology. And last but not least, uh Michael Ameling, president of uh SAP Business Technology Platform, and member of SAP Extended Board. Which means today we will talk about
enterprise-wide automation as not just experience, as product itself within the enterprise. Please welcome the panel with a round of applause, please. >> So, hello, ladies and gentlemen. Now we are
bringing together an unlikely but all the more exciting pair. We've already heard we are joined today by Michael Ameling, president of SAP Business Technology Platform, and by Axel Shell,
who is the CTO of Allianz Technology. And let us start with a little challenge for you. Could you summarize what you your company is doing that is of
relevance to us today one sentence? Is that possible? >> So, where do we start? In one sentence, good challenge. So, I think I would summarize it as
instead of running big moonshots and shooting for the moon, we try to create a kind of a gen AI-enabled organization. I'm happy to explain later what it means.
>> Okay. Thank you. I think you succeeded in that first one. What about you? >> Yeah, looking at SAP, I think with more than 300 million users
using this worldwide, there's a lot to do in terms to customize and basically develop from the agentic world also for our customers. And this is where you all can help and
where you all can contribute to. >> So, at first, let us set the stage a little bit. Many people in this audience might have automated a task or a team,
maybe even a department. But, we talked about it previously, automating an entire enterprise is not just more of the same, but an an entirely different
story. How come? >> Yeah, let me let let me start shortly. And I mean, you you said it. We're talking about an enterprise. And I think
we all agree with AI and technology and auto automation, you can very rapidly automate processes, develop certain applications, and the like. But, one thing I learned when starting
at SAP, is that you're dealing with multinational companies working really across the globe, dealing with thousands of IT systems, dealing with let's say a supply chain or let's say a
procurement across the entire globe. And then suddenly it's getting a little bit more complex. So, we are talking about topics like compliance, like certifications,
uh security, and all these topics which come on top basically of, let us say, so typical development task, but really to do this at scale with enterprise
readiness. And keeping that in mind, I mean, developing at an enterprise, I mean, it also needs to run for the long term. It needs basically fit basically
enterprise requirements of any of these multinational or, let's say, bigger customers and the like. >> Mhm. >> Uh and this is, of course, a lot of
challenges on top what you usually do maybe as a developer in the first hand. >> Mhm. >> Yeah. Uh and I think this is what we
need to keep in mind when we talk about AI or automation and the like. So, how can it be, for example, deterministic for a company? Because I think you all
agree when you have your invoices that you want to have them 100% correct. Or let's look at your salary statements. Of course, I think you all agree, I mean,
it can be correct or not, yeah? You want to have a very deterministic approach. So, running an enterprise uh at scale comes with, let's say, a lot of
additional requirements uh which need to run at scale with uh secure. And I think this is one of the key themes I would like to bring in here.
>> Very convincing examples. Uh Alex, you nodded your head. >> So, yeah, I mean, you already said um key important topics like compliance and governance and
repeatability of processes. I I think the the key differences or one of the key differences, I would say, first layer is if you have
different lines of business with different business models. They have different needs, different capabilities. Number two is if you look into various regions, you come with
different requirements in terms of uh governance, but also regulation. The third layer is capabilities. People and also teams have different capabilities and offer different conviction. So, are
they already convinced to do X, Y, Z? And last but not least, I would really also like to to come up with the challenge of
prioritization. You cannot do everything at the same time. So, the really tough point is to say no. To say like, this is the current focus, less is more. We
don't do 27 things at the same time, even not able to focus on anything. Um that's a key challenge. Um we have internally the the saying like, you need
to say 1,000 times no before you will say one time yes. That's a bit the recipe to create simplicity. If you have a lot of
complexity, you're not able to scale. Large enterprises are a lot about scalability. And the the let's say the enemy of scalability is complexity because you cannot scale complexity.
That's impossible. So, in order to harmonize and scale, you need to find the key, the secret to simplicity. And that's saying a lot of times no.
>> Mhm. Now, we are wondering, of course, how do you set the right priorities? Where have you said no, and where have you said yes?
>> So, it starts with couple of surrounding factors. You need to look at your your business, how it's developing, what are the challenges out there from a
market perspective. You need to also compare yourself, of course, with competitors is understanding what's going on. Second one is you need to understand market
dynamics. What is happening, for example, for an insurance industry it's very important to understand what's going out there with a pulley prices. We see the wars going on, we see the
demographical change, we see climate impact. So, that that is another factor that you need to reflect. And then last but not least, of course, you also look
into all kinds of economical factors. So, what brings the biggest business benefit? I mean, you have goals like you want to either grow or be more
profitable. That drives another area of capabilities. And then last but not least, I would also say like, you need to find a way how AI
strengthens your strategy. >> Mhm. >> And that's a tough one because the strategy is also evolving, AI is evolving, the capabilities evolve, but you need to find a way how those two
work together. So, you cannot separate your AI transformation from your strategy. >> Mhm. Um >> I mean maybe let me double double down on that one because I mean fully echo on
that one and I would like to to add one additional perspective and looking inside and outside, I think one thing you also need to agree on, where do you
want to differentiate? >> Mhm. >> Yeah, so because you set the priorities, think about also what you should do and what you should let others do. So, for
example, I mean we have a large also partner ecosystem, yeah, and I mean looking also in this round here, I mean see a lot of partners also at these
booths. Uh we also decided very consciously where we say, "No, this is not our core strength. This is not our core competence. This is where for
example, we let uh their IDEs for example out there. Let's look at it from a developer perspective, right? So, where we do partnerships uh and this is
something which we don't compete. >> Mhm. >> Uh but then there are other topics for example, bringing context into the business, yeah? So, what for example are
the right domain models to access an SAP system for example? This is something where we can bring actually more value. And the same for our customers. So,
looking at the customer perspective, of course, each company has different requirements where they want to do optimize. Maybe in manufacturing, maybe in their supply chain and the like. And
this is something where you need to be very clear from the beginning on, where are your investments, where you want to differentiate, and this is where you may
apply AI, where you want to strengthen your automation and the like. And there are other topics where you might think, "Oh, let's partner over here." Or maybe
that's something where we can use commodity and the like. So, that's very very important to understand what is your strengths and where do you want to
truly want to differentiate. >> Yeah. Um talking about making the right choices, SAP announced that it will shift more from um applications that are
bolted onto um AI to yeah, like to um design tools that are natively built around artificial intelligence. How does it look like in like with the real customer's example in
a supply chain, in the finance branch? And where is the value really created? Are we speaking mostly of um creating new business models, speed,
about the reduction of errors? >> Yeah. Yeah, maybe let me bring one perspective. And yes, 2 3 years ago, I mean, we started also with our systems.
I'm not sure how many people are aware of SAP, but basically I have solutions in terms of procurement, human capital to management, finance, of course, so
across the entire value chain uh of our customers. So, within these solutions, we also started to build in, as you said it, AI within the
applications. So, for example, the idea of an assistant or you have certain automations in place or you can imagine in invoicing that uh invoices are
automatically checked or even basically are processed and the like. And now, meanwhile, just recently at uh in May we launched the autonomous enterprise. So,
the vision where we want to go to is that you really have autonomous agents running across the different domains, so in HR, in procurement, in supply chain
management, and the like, who run your business. And as the idea behind is, of course, that with AI, you can autonomously run with agents certain of
these processes. >> Yeah. >> Now, what does it mean? You need to rethink business processes. You started in the beginning with automation. Yeah, I mean, of course,
automation exists for quite a long time. You had workflow, robotic process automation, and the like. But with AI and agents, you need to rethink
processes. So, it's not about No, just simply automating what you had before. You also need to rethink business processes to come really to this
autonomous vision. Yeah, so there a bunch of new capabilities which you can make use of. So, that for example, finance, it does not only automate a
certain process, it rethinks how finance works. So, for example, to automate your cash flow into like and this is of course what we bring to the customers.
>> Yeah. Not every agent project is successful. Could you give us a little insight into what the most common reasons are that these agents fail?
And what are key success factors? >> So, I would say it starts with the project setup. So, first of all, did you define proper
ownership? Is ownership linked to a person? Is ownership linked to the success of a person? Is ownership linked to a steering committee? So, steering committee not a good idea
from my point of view. So, >> Why? >> Um I think you you in order to be successful, you need to really have exactly those ownerships.
Um I'm less interested in from a sponsorship who signs the check for the certain project. I'm interested in who will be the one who makes it happen. Who
is the one who takes the decisions, the call, and is also responsible for the impact. Um another source of success or not success from my point of view is if
something goes wrong, do you learn from the mistake or do you try to find out who was accountable for that? If you try to find the accountable
person, it takes forever and sets the wrong culture. So, you need to find out what went wrong. Another one is running multiple initiatives in parallel
is better than thinking a long time about should I do it or not. >> Okay. >> If you don't do it, you don't learn. You
don't create any data points what could be done or could not be done. If you do it something fast, you make mistakes, things go wrong, but
you learn a lot and you have the data points where you know this is a good idea and this is not a good idea. So, it
comes together with really um doing a couple of things in parallel, of course focused and prioritized, but clear ownership is for me the most
important one I check when the team runs a project. >> Mhm. And because you mentioned that things can go wrong, I mean, who is accountable if mistakes
happen that actually cost money? >> So, of course somebody is always accountable, but I think this you need to create a culture where teams
take the responsibility without finding out who is accountable or who is responsible for the mistakes. Um and you need to create this culture where mistakes are totally okay, learn
from it. Um you need to have a clever system where you control the blast radius of mistakes. I mean, a mistake is not the same as a mistake. You can make
a big mistake which can can bring the company into trouble, that's not of course a good idea, but you you can like lots of mistakes and you can revise
decisions because you can easily take them back, you can change the setup tomorrow. Um these are the, let's say, anchoring points I would follow on less the
who does it and of course people need to understand what kind of risk they take and what kind of blast radius they work on.
>> Mhm. >> Yep. Yeah, thanks for that and let me let me two perspectives on that and one is more technical one. >> Mhm.
>> So, for example, in a lot of AI projects, I mean, you need to do your homework. And what do I mean with that? I mean, I
saw the slogan back there, in out, right? So, if you don't get basically your homework and having access to the right data. Uh also in the
security layer, for example, if you want to create an assistance, of course you need identity management, for example. Yeah? Also, when you connect to the
systems, you need to do integration. So basically just focusing on AI and without doing your homework, for example, updating your systems, yeah, having a a landscape where you have
access to the and the right governance, for example, in place to access your data. Having a proper homogeneous layer, for example, to access your data objects
and the like. Without that, AI won't work, yeah, because it will have the same troubles as you have as a human being. Where do I find the data? What is
the right security? Where do what do I have access to and the like? So, you need to modernize also your landscape and your systems and the like. So, you
need to you do your homework. This doesn't go away. That's number one. Um number two, also from uh let's say implementation perspective, you asked
what what what does fail? I mean, you also need to understand what you're doing. If you use AI, and let me take a very
provocative example, uh you had a workflow before which was deterministic and very, I don't know, let's say you're in the approval process, and now you put AI on top. I
mean, great. You now use AI to simply do what the workflow did before, but now it's non-deterministic, so it's actually actually worse than before,
right? And actually, you're even more expensive because you're burning tokens for something which was fully automated before. Yeah, so AI is not the answer for
everything. Let's keep this in mind. Yeah, if you have a workflow uh and you can do that, I mean, it's cheap, it's deterministic, do it. So, please really
think about which problem you want to solve and how to use this. So, this is where some projects also fail. Hey, the the outcome is not better. Yeah, sure. I
mean, you automated what was automated before. And then you said about the responsibility. Uh so, for example, what we said from the beginning, and actually, I don't
know, SAP was one of the first who had a let's say an um a code of conduct and also for AI uh even in 2018 already, where we said,
"Okay, for whatever comes in place, there are certain things which we should we don't do, right? So, being responsible, for example, I mean firing people with AI of
course this is something which we which you won't see in any of these systems. Uh but of course there's always a human in the loop. So what we decided on for a
lot of processes that there is a factor where human is informed where the decision is voted as you said it, somebody needs to be responsible in the
end and somebody needs to have oversight and which comes me to the last point. Uh I think what comes more more important uh however I know some some companies
also over here is you need to have the traceability and the monitoring place. You need to understand what is happening. So monitoring and uh this
entire observability across your IT stack is more important than ever because you want to trace basically if something went wrong, which decision was taken by when. So this is something I
would urge every developer to look into. Uh do you really understand what is happening and do you have the ability to see what really happened? Yeah, so maybe
some advice in that perspective. >> Many interesting points. I hope we can pick up some of these still. And both of you mentioned that enterprise-wide
automation is not only a technological issue, but maybe more so even an accountability or like an organizational issue. To what extent do you think it is
which? >> It's for sure not an IT project. Uh it has to be driven by the business. It cannot be led by top management. I mean what really helps
looking at successful transformations, what helps is if top management is supporting the the vision, the strategy is clearly laid out, but you need to find a way how business
drives those activities. I think many of the AI transformations have this touch of let's do this IT project. Um and then you run into multiple
problems. Also building on what you said with approval workflows and stuff like just an easy example. How many of you do expense travel expense approvals? And
theoretically this is something where you need the human in the loop to check it. But we should ask ourselves how good can we do
it? I mean if I have a travel expense approval, can I check is the restaurant existing? Does the Wiener Schnitzel cost 23 euros? >> Probably yes.
>> How many people exactly were there? So so how how should I check all of this? Either I trust or I believe or and and
that there can be multiple solutions to the problem, but I would assume that many of the travel expenses at the moment would not discover a receipt of a
restaurant that is not existing. >> Mhm. >> I like the example by the way. So >> [laughter] >> yes, I mean >> We have a KPI that more or less is
how many travel expense approvals manually do we have to do in the system? And that from my point of view it should be like three a year for me. And it's
not that yet, but that's I think the target which is difficult to achieve, but it's a good example where you can a bit substitute the human in the loop with a
clever solution. >> Mhm. >> And I mean to build on that I mean you mentioned this this business and LOB. Yes, I can only echo that. I mean in the
end whatever we do yeah and yes we it's very developer focused, but in the end we are solving business problems. Yeah, so we really need to understand
what's the line of business or let's say individual task basically want to improve. Like I said before, is it do we want to optimize cash flow? Yeah, do we
want to optimize something in our supply chain? Do we want to optimize traveling for example yeah and the like and the receipt handling and the like and
this is something which is very very important. And yes sometimes we have a too technical view in all honesty yeah where we go in okay we have the solution
already before we discuss basically the business problem. And I think this is where we need to start with. And then with AI and A talking about agents, I
want to give one more more additional perspective. Because often when we have agents and AI, we we talk about evils, right? So, how can we check if a certain agent
basically is exactly doing what we want and intend to? I want to lift it to one level above. We also need to understand how does it perform on your business?
So, what I talk about, for example, if you have a business process like in procurement, yeah, or lead to cash, that there are certain business process
performance indicators. This is what they called. >> Yeah. >> Uh and in the end, you need to understand does whatever I developed, yeah, maybe in robotic process
automation, maybe a workflow, or maybe an agent, does it really come to the business outcome I intended in the beginning? And this is very important
because as business evolves, uh but this is really important to understand, and this comes me again back to this observability topic, you need to
understand as a developer, not only what you developed, how this operates, how this runs, also how this performs truly on your business, yeah, which is
an additional challenge to what we have seen before, but this is utmost important because in the end, as I said it, you need to have this correlation
because obviously you're burning also some money in terms of infrastructure, of course AI tokens and whatever, so that it really basically performs as you
intended to. >> Yeah, yeah. And what are the typical measurements or things that you measure, dimensions that you think are quite reliable indicators for measuring
whether this is working or not? >> Yeah, as I said, I mean, uh usually what we have, so for example, we have a solution called SAP Signavio,
which is defining basically uh you do basically process mining and the like. And with that said, within this one, we have defined 2,000 business processes
basically is running across the the entire value chain of a company. And for each of them, the existing two to three business performance performance
indicators, yeah? So, for example, like cash flow optimization, yeah? Or how long does it take until an invoice is paid, for example? How many, I don't
know, menu steps, for example, in a certain process are basically activated and the like. And this is basically what you need to monitor. And this is what you
basically evaluate against basically in order to really understand the outcome of basically what you have developed. >> And this is something that doesn't necessarily get easier if you're such an
international organization, Axel, for example like Allianz. How does enterprise-wide automation work in an international multinational company? Yes, if you could give us an insight.
>> So, I mean, it's the way how you collaborate. Our strategy is platform strategy, so we try to leverage platforms wherever possible. We try to set up the easier pieces like
infrastructure in a global way, so that, I don't know, wherever you go, in which country you are, you can log into the network, use the telephone there, if you
still have one. Um cloud infrastructure is kind of scaled and harmonized, and then of course, it comes to people, how they work together in an international company. I mean,
it's not that super specific. We work in lines of business, and then of course, cluster in kind of agile setups, where in the future AI will also change
the way how we work in those teams. Um And and then I think there is no no magic recipe. You work with a couple of
architectural guardrails that you want to follow, and then harmonization through our something as a key strategy. We'd like to implement stuff somewhere, if it
works, scale it, and then roll it out in other countries. That that makes the organization fast, and don't run into this problem everybody needs to reinvent.
Our slogan is more like copy with pride. If somebody has done something that is great, just copy with pride. Much better than to come up with a new idea that we
already had before. >> I really like that slogan. And what influence does it have that you're working in such a highly regulated industry? >> It's tough and good at the same time.
So, it's tough because sometimes I wake up in the morning and tell myself like how cool would it be if I work in a non-regulated retail
industry. I would do so many things really differently. And then the other side I think a lot of stuff that we do really make sense to I
don't know orchestrate processes in a certain way and have kind of third-party risk management available, whatever. Of course, as a multinational many country regulated
industry, you you need certain guardrails. Unfortunately, fortunately, it's the same. Um I I think the key is to have smart governance in place. You can do this
kind of in a clever and in a stupid way. The stupid way is whenever you do something, you need to fill out the 30
forms and make sure everything is documented. You're super slow. Smart governance works in a way that the activity triggers already a couple of things. You don't need to think about
users don't need to think too much about it. So, if you work on a platform, the platform already has lots of controls that come with it. So, you don't need to
ask each and every user to think about his own controls or the teams. Um that that's I think a tough challenge. Um as I said, it's good and bad at the same
time. I I feel we are walking a bit in the direction of having really a lot of regulation. If I just look 5 years back,
things have changed significantly. I mean, as an IT person, you now have a governance and regulation regulatory expert. That was different 5 years ago.
>> We >> Can Can I add one point because on regulations you triggered me. >> I mean, yes, of course. I mean, you need
to think about how serving in all different countries with all the different regulations you have or maybe in Europe, in US, in China, and the
like. And there comes this additional perspective now of sovereignty on top. Uh and now basically you can imagine if you build a software platform which
needs to run globally, uh you need to run on different hyperscalers, yeah, from AWS to GCP to Ali Cloud own data centers. Now suddenly
you have now additional different models and LLMs which are also with regional different availability, right? So, you can use different models you can obviously in US, in China, in Europe,
right? And now then comes this data sovereignty. So, for example, you need to run uh cloud in country, for example. And this is what I meant in the beginning
also with enterprise grail. So, these are all different dimension which you as a developer you need to consider from the beginning on. Yeah, and when you
want to basically run a software which runs at scale in a global environment, right? So, basically you have additional factors now not only with let's say the
hyperscalers but also now with the different models and now with the different sovereignty requirements. And this is something which you need to think of from the beginning when you
start developing something. >> Adding another layer of complexity, we are unfortunately coming to an end. So, as a last question to you, I would love
to know how close are we actually to enterprise-wide automation and to what extent is it still more of a promise? >> So, I think there's three steps. First, you
have to crawl, then you can walk, and then you can run. The companies who try to jump something from crawling to running doesn't work. And everybody
needs to understand where I am in the journey. Crawl, walk, run. The run is the toughest part and it takes also a long time to practice.
So, I think there is no overall story. Every company has a different status and maturity level. >> Mhm. What about Allianz? >> We're somewhere in the middle.
>> Okay. >> Always humble, of course. >> Yeah, of course. >> Yeah, [snorts] this just brings me back to do your homework. Yeah, I mean
according to Gartner, I mean 80% of the companies already using AI, but only 20% roughly basically use it really at scale. Yeah, I mean I can see
of course we as SAP also we do it and looking also at 35,000 up to 40,000 developers, I mean you have a lot of AI
already in place which helps us tremendously. I mean most of the developers don't write code directly anymore. They use a genetic stuff and the like. So I see really AI at scale,
but is there still a lot of potential? Absolutely. And this is why it's so exciting. It's so exciting being here actually because this is what we all
basically work for. So there are some exciting times and a lot of potential ahead of us. >> Beautiful finishing words. Thank you so much for the insights you gave us. Thank
you. >> Thank you. >> [applause]
